syllabus_version.title: CBSE Curriculum for the Academic Year 2026-27

chapters.title: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation

topics.title: Beginnings and subsistence strategies

concepts.learning_objective: Students will identify the Early, Mature and Late Harappan phases and their approximate dates.
Students will explain how archaeologists reconstruct Harappan diet from plant and animal remains.
Students will interpret the evidence for ploughing, cropping and irrigation in Harappan agriculture.

topics.title: Mohenjodaro: a planned urban centre

concepts.learning_objective: Students will describe the Citadel, the Lower Town and the standardised bricks as signs of planning.
Students will explain how the drainage system reflects town planning.
Students will describe domestic architecture and the structures on the Citadel, including the Great Bath.

topics.title: Tracking social differences

concepts.learning_objective: Students will evaluate what Harappan burials reveal, and do not reveal, about social differences.
Students will distinguish utilitarian objects from luxuries and interpret their distribution.

topics.title: Finding out about craft production

concepts.learning_objective: Students will describe the materials and techniques used to make Harappan beads.
Students will identify the evidence archaeologists use to locate centres of craft production.

topics.title: Strategies for procuring materials

concepts.learning_objective: Students will explain how the Harappans obtained raw materials from within the subcontinent.
Students will analyse the evidence for Harappan contact with Oman, Dilmun and Mesopotamia.

topics.title: Seals, script and weights

concepts.learning_objective: Students will explain how seals and sealings were used in long-distance communication.
Students will state the known features of the undeciphered Harappan script.
Students will apply the binary and decimal pattern of Harappan weights.

topics.title: Ancient authority and the end of the civilisation

concepts.learning_objective: Students will analyse the evidence for authority and the debate on rulers in Harappan society.
Students will explain the changes after c. 1900 BCE and the explanations offered for the decline.
Students will evaluate how re-examination of evidence changed the interpretation of an 'invasion'.

topics.title: Discovering the civilisation and problems of interpretation

concepts.learning_objective: Students will trace the roles of Cunningham, Sahni, Banerji and Marshall in discovering the civilisation.
Students will explain stratigraphy and how excavation methods affect the recovery of context.
Students will evaluate the difficulties of reconstructing Harappan religious practices.

chapters.title: Kings, Farmers and Towns: Early States and Economies (c. 600 BCE-600 CE)

topics.title: Prinsep and Piyadassi: inscriptions as sources

concepts.learning_objective: Recall how James Prinsep's decipherment of Brahmi and Kharosthi in the 1830s changed the study of early Indian political history.
Explain what inscriptions are, the languages they used and how undated inscriptions are dated.

topics.title: The earliest states: mahajanapadas and Magadha

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the main features of the sixteen mahajanapadas, including monarchies, ganas or sanghas and fortified capitals.
Compare the explanations of modern historians and early Buddhist and Jaina writers for the rise of Magadha.

topics.title: An early empire: the Mauryas

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the sources used to reconstruct Mauryan history and what Asoka meant by dhamma.
Explain how the Mauryan Empire was administered through political centres, routes, the army and dhamma mahamattas.
Evaluate how important the Mauryan Empire was and why historians in colonial India valued it.

topics.title: New notions of kingship

concepts.learning_objective: Distinguish chiefs from kings and describe the chiefdoms of the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas in Tamilakam.
Explain how the Kushanas used titles, statues and coins to project divine kingship.
Explain the role of samantas and assess prashastis such as the Prayaga Prashasti as historical sources.

topics.title: A changing countryside: subjects and agricultural production

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how historians use stories such as the Jatakas to understand what subjects thought of their rulers.
Describe plough agriculture, transplantation and irrigation as strategies for raising production, and their limits.

topics.title: Differences in rural society and land grants

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the categories of rural people named in Pali and Sangam texts, including the gahapati.
Analyse land grants, agraharas and the historians' debate on their impact.

topics.title: Towns and trade

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the location of early historic towns and the evidence of their elites, craftspersons and guilds.
Explain the land, river and sea routes of trade within the subcontinent and beyond.
Analyse what punch-marked, Indo-Greek, Kushana, Yaudheya and Gupta coins reveal about exchange.

topics.title: Deciphering inscriptions and their limitations

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how Brahmi and Kharosthi were deciphered and how epigraphists identify the issuer of an inscription.
Evaluate the technical and fundamental limitations of inscriptional evidence.

chapters.title: Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies (c. 600 BCE-600 CE)

topics.title: The Critical Edition of the Mahabharata

concepts.learning_objective: Describe how the Critical Edition of the Mahabharata was prepared between 1919 and 1966.
Explain what the regional variations in Mahabharata manuscripts reveal about social history.

topics.title: Kinship and Marriage: Many Rules and Varied Practices

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the ideal of patriliny and its importance for succession in ruling families.
Distinguish between exogamy, endogamy, polygyny and polyandry and the Brahmanical forms of marriage.
Analyse how Satavahana inscriptions show departures from Brahmanical gotra rules.

topics.title: Social Differences: Within and Beyond the Framework of Caste

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the occupations prescribed for the four varnas and stories that upheld them.
Evaluate the evidence that political power did not depend on Kshatriya birth.
Explain the nature of jatis, guilds and the treatment of groups placed outside the varna order.

topics.title: Beyond Birth: Resources and Status

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how access to property differed between men and women.
Analyse how the Buddhist tradition questioned status based on varna by pointing to wealth.
Interpret Sangam poems that show chiefs were expected to share their resources.

topics.title: Explaining Social Differences: A Social Contract

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the Buddhist myth of the mahasammata in the Sutta Pitaka.
Evaluate the implications of the idea that kingship rested on human choice.

topics.title: Handling Texts: Historians and the Mahabharata

concepts.learning_objective: Distinguish the narrative and didactic sections of the Mahabharata and the meaning of itihasa.
Identify the authors and phases of composition of the Mahabharata.
Evaluate how historians compare the epic with archaeological and social evidence.

topics.title: A Dynamic Text

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the Mahabharata grew through versions, retellings and performances.
Analyse how Mahashweta Devi's retelling raises questions the Sanskrit text is silent on.

chapters.title: Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings: Cultural Developments (c. 600 BCE - 600 CE)

topics.title: A glimpse of Sanchi and the sources

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the rulers of Bhopal and later decisions helped preserve the stupa complex at Sanchi.
Identify the textual and material sources historians use to reconstruct religious ideas of c. 600 BCE - 600 CE.

topics.title: The background: sacrifices and debates

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the early Vedic sacrificial tradition and how sacrifices changed over time.
Explain the new questions about life, rebirth and ultimate reality raised in the Upanishads.
Distinguish the Ajivika and Lokayata positions and explain how historians know about them.

topics.title: The message of Mahavira and the spread of Jainism

concepts.learning_objective: State the central teachings of Jainism, including ahimsa, karma and the five vows.
Describe how Jaina literature and sculpture spread and were preserved.

topics.title: The Buddha, his teachings and Buddhist texts

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how historians reconstruct the Buddha's life from hagiographies and assess their value.
Explain the Buddhist ideas of anicca, anatta, dukkha, the middle path and nibbana.
Identify the three pitakas and how Buddhist texts were compiled, transmitted and preserved.

topics.title: Followers of the Buddha and the sangha

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the organisation, membership and functioning of the Buddhist sangha.
Explain the entry of women into the sangha and interpret verses of the Therigatha.
Analyse why Buddhism appealed to many people in a time of social change.

topics.title: Stupas: why and how they were built

concepts.learning_objective: Identify chaityas and the places associated with the Buddha's life that came to be regarded as sacred.
Explain why stupas were built and why they were venerated.
Describe the structure of a stupa and the patrons who financed its building.

topics.title: Discovering stupas and reading their sculpture

concepts.learning_objective: Compare the fate of the stupas at Amaravati and Sanchi after their discovery.
Interpret symbols used in early Buddhist sculpture by relating them to textual traditions.
Analyse how popular and pre-Buddhist traditions shaped the sculpture at Sanchi.

topics.title: New religious traditions and the limits of what we can see

concepts.learning_objective: Explain the changes in Buddhist ideas and practices that led to Mahayana Buddhism.
Describe the growth of Vaishnavism, Shaivism, the Puranas and early temple architecture.
Evaluate the problems historians face in interpreting unfamiliar images and images that texts do not explain.
